shortcut_name: direct reduction to 3-coloring with naive lexicographic DFS
evidence: "for c in (1, 2, 3)"; "if color[nb] == c"; "color = [0] * n # 0 = unassigned, else 1..3"
affordance_in_statement: Each component i must be assigned a discrete state vector V_i, chosen from exactly one of three available vectors: A = (1, 1, 0), B = (1, 0, 1), or C = (0, 1, 1). ... the state vectors assigned to any interacting pair must have a dot product of exactly 1.
secondary_shortcut_name: enumerating colors in increasing order makes the first DFS solution lexicographically smallest
removal_suggestion: There is no wording-only removal while preserving the task: the three vectors have dot product 1 exactly when they are distinct, so the core problem is intrinsically 3-colorability. If only presentation may change, describe the interaction rule indirectly through an opaque overlap-score definition rather than exposing the three vectors and their pairwise products, while retaining the same semantics.

survivor_shortcuts.shortcut: Treats each vector as one of three colors and rejects equal colors on every edge, using increasing color order for lexicographic output.
survivor_shortcuts.affordance: the three listed vectors together with the requirement that every interacting pair has dot product exactly 1

survivor_shortcuts.shortcut: Recognizes the vector compatibility relation as a three-coloring constraint and searches assignments over colors 1, 2, and 3.
survivor_shortcuts.affordance: A, B, and C are the only available vectors and interacting pairs must have dot product exactly 1

survivor_shortcuts.shortcut: Uses a DFS over color values 1..3, relying on the fact that equal vectors are forbidden while distinct vectors are allowed.
survivor_shortcuts.affordance: the explicit three-state vector domain and pairwise dot-product condition

common_affordance: The explicit three-vector dot-product relation collapses the problem to ordinary 3-coloring: distinct vectors have dot product 1 and identical vectors have dot product 2.

defeated_student_causes.why_failed: Its compatibility handling did not correctly implement the required relation between equal and distinct states; the shown dot-product reasoning was not carried through into a correct assignment procedure.

recommended_edit: Re-present the state interaction rule indirectly as an opaque overlap-score predicate, without explicitly exposing that all three distinct state pairs satisfy the condition and equal pairs do not. This is the only plausible single presentation edit targeting the reduction shared by all survivors; a truly robust change would require changing the underlying task rather than its wording.
regression_risk: Making the compatibility rule more explicit or supplying a compatibility table could restore glm-5 by fixing its state-relation mistake.
